lines: The most consistent finding across all experimental conditions is that temporal context improves probe precision and reduces FPR, regardless of signal modality. \cref{fig:window_ablation} shows this pattern for R1-8B; precision and FPR gains hold across all three models, though balanced accuracy improvement is model-dependent.
+\fbox{\parbox{0.9\columnwidth}{\centering\vspace{2em}[Window ablation plot: Precision and FPR vs.\ window size $W$ for R1-8B HS probes]\vspace{2em}}}

+\caption{Effect of temporal window size on R1-8B HS probe performance. Precision increases monotonically from 69.3\% ($W{=}1$) to 82.2\% ($W{=}25$); FPR decreases from 9.65\% to 4.83\%. Coverage decreases as larger windows make the probe more conservative.}

On R1-8B, increasing window size from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$ improves balanced accuracy from 77.8\% to 81.0\% (+3.2pp), precision from 69.3\% to 82.2\% (+12.9pp), and reduces step-level FPR from 9.65\% to 4.83\% ($-$4.8pp). QwQ-32B shows a similar monotonic pattern (+3.2pp accuracy, +7.4pp precision, $-$5.9pp FPR from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$). R1-32B exhibits a non-monotonic trajectory: accuracy peaks at $W{=}10$ then declines below the $W{=}1$ baseline by $W{=}25$ (71.8\% $\rightarrow$ 70.3\%), though precision and FPR still improve (+1.7pp, $-$5.5pp). Across all three models, FPR consistently decreases with larger windows (\cref{tab:temporal_main}). Larger windows make probes more conservative: fewer traces cross the detection threshold (coverage decreases from 72.1\% to 48.8\% on R1-8B under $K{=}1$ criterion), but those that do are classified with higher confidence.

The coverage-quality trade-off depends on the detection criterion. Under $K{=}1$ (single threshold crossing), larger $W$ reduces coverage because the smoothed probe score crosses the boundary fewer times. Under stricter criteria ($K{=}5$, requiring consecutive crossings), larger $W$ can improve effective coverage by eliminating transient false crossings. We report $K{=}1$ results throughout for interpretability, noting that deployment systems would tune $K$ alongside $W$.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate contrastive trace probes across three reasoning models (R1-8B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B), two signal modalities (hidden states and text), and multiple temporal aggregation strategies. Our experiments address four questions: (1) How much does temporal context improve detection? (2) Does the choice of signal modality matter? (3) Can sequence models detect unsafe reasoning earlier? (4) Do probes transfer across models?
5	
6	\subsection{Temporal Context as Primary Factor}
7	\label{sec:temporal_primary}
8	
9	The most consistent finding across all experimental conditions is that temporal context improves probe precision and reduces FPR, regardless of signal modality. \cref{fig:window_ablation} shows this pattern for R1-8B; precision and FPR gains hold across all three models, though balanced accuracy improvement is model-dependent.
10	
11	\begin{figure}[t]
12	\centering
13	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_temporal_improvement.pdf}
14	\caption{Effect of temporal window size on R1-8B HS probe performance. Precision increases monotonically from 69.3\% ($W{=}1$) to 82.2\% ($W{=}25$); FPR decreases from 9.65\% to 4.83\%. Coverage decreases as larger windows make the probe more conservative.}
15	\label{fig:window_ablation}
16	\end{figure}
17	
18	On R1-8B, increasing window size from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$ improves balanced accuracy from 77.8\% to 81.0\% (+3.2pp), precision from 69.3\% to 82.2\% (+12.9pp), and reduces step-level FPR from 9.65\% to 4.83\% ($-$4.8pp). QwQ-32B shows a similar monotonic pattern (+3.2pp accuracy, +7.4pp precision, $-$5.9pp FPR from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$). R1-32B exhibits a non-monotonic trajectory: accuracy peaks at $W{=}10$ then declines below the $W{=}1$ baseline by $W{=}25$ (71.8\% $\rightarrow$ 70.3\%), though precision and FPR still improve (+1.7pp, $-$5.5pp). Across all three models, FPR consistently decreases with larger windows (\cref{tab:temporal_main}). Larger windows make probes more conservative: fewer traces cross the detection threshold (coverage decreases from 72.1\% to 48.8\% on R1-8B under $K{=}1$ criterion), but those that do are classified with higher confidence.
19	
20	The coverage-quality trade-off depends on the detection criterion. Under $K{=}1$ (single threshold crossing), larger $W$ reduces coverage because the smoothed probe score crosses the boundary fewer times. Under stricter criteria ($K{=}5$, requiring consecutive crossings), larger $W$ can improve effective coverage by eliminating transient false crossings. We report $K{=}1$ results throughout for interpretability, noting that deployment systems would tune $K$ alongside $W$.
21	
22	The key observation is that the magnitude of temporal improvement on precision (+1.7 to +12.9pp) and FPR ($-$4.8 to $-$5.9pp) dwarfs the modality gap (0 to 7pp FPR difference in the strongest case). Temporal context is modality-agnostic: whether probes read hidden activations or generated text, observing multiple reasoning steps provides the dominant source of discriminative information for FPR reduction.

Linear probes have become a standard tool for investigating what information neural networks encode in their intermediate representations. \citet{alain2017understanding} introduced the technique of training linear classifiers on intermediate layers to understand learned representations, establishing the foundational methodology. \citet{belinkov2017morphology} applied this approach to neural machine translation, showing that different layers specialize in different linguistic levels (morphology in lower layers, semantics in upper layers). \citet{conneau2018probing} extended probing to sentence-level embeddings, designing a suite of tasks that isolate specific linguistic properties and demonstrating that fixed-size representations capture hierarchical structure beyond surface statistics. \citet{belinkov2019analysis} provide a comprehensive survey of these probing methods across architectures. \citet{hewitt2019structural} demonstrate that syntax trees can be recovered from contextual embeddings through a linear transformation, establishing that rich structural information is linearly accessible in pretrained representations. A key methodological concern is whether probes genuinely detect learned structure or merely memorize the task. \citet{hewitt2019control} address this by introducing control tasks and the selectivity metric (probe accuracy minus control accuracy), providing a principled way to distinguish true decodability from probe expressiveness. Our work extends probing from linguistic attributes to safety-relevant properties: we train temporal probes on hidden states to detect when a reasoning model commits to unsafe behavior, and we adopt the control task methodology of \citet{hewitt2019control} to validate that our probes capture genuine safety commitment signals rather than superficial patterns.
